posts.title: Money Laundering: How Criminals Use a Bank
posts.excerpt: Team assignment: explain one method of money laundering. Our example is Danske Bank in Estonia, where around 200 billion euros passed through one small branch.

blocks.label: Assignment
content: Explain one method of money laundering.

A bank is often needed for money laundering. Criminals need a way to move large amounts of money through the financial system so that it looks legal. One well-known example is **Danske Bank in Estonia**.

Between **2007 and 2015**, around **200 billion euros** from foreign customers passed through one small branch of the bank. Many of these customers were **shell companies**: companies that exist on paper but have no real business. The bank later admitted that many of these payments were probably suspicious.

A manager called **Howard Wilkinson** became suspicious because one company moved huge amounts of money, even though its records showed no assets. He reported this internally in **2013**. His reports later helped uncover the whole case.
In **2022**, Danske Bank pleaded guilty in the United States and had to pay around **2 billion US dollars**.

blocks.label: Key terms
content: - **Money laundering:** making money from crime look like it comes from a legal source.
- **Shell company:** a company that exists only on paper and has no real business activity.
- **Whistleblower:** an employee who reports wrongdoing inside their own organisation.

questions.q: Roughly how much money flowed through Danske Bank's small Estonian branch?
questions.explain: Around €200 billion passed through the branch between 2007 and 2015.

questions.q: What is a shell company?
options: A company that only exists on paper
questions.explain: Shell companies have no real business, which makes them useful for hiding where money comes from.

questions.q: Who helped uncover the case?
questions.explain: Howard Wilkinson, a manager at the bank, reported his suspicions in 2013.

posts.title: Memecoins Explained in One Minute
posts.excerpt: FMA task: explain one financial term in one minute. Memecoins are cryptocurrencies born from internet jokes and trends, and they can rise and crash very fast.

blocks.label: Assignment
content: FMA challenge: explain one term in one minute.
Memecoins are cryptocurrencies that often start from an internet joke or trend, for example **PepeCoin** or **Banana Coin**. Their value can rise very quickly, but it can crash just as fast.
Many people buy them when everyone is talking about them, and then lose money as soon as the hype is over.
Bitcoin is different. It was the **first crypto asset**, its supply is limited to **21 million coins**, and many people see it as **digital gold**.

Memecoins are mostly about **speculation**. They often have no clear purpose, and sometimes there is even fraud behind them. That is why you should never invest just because of big promises of profit.

questions.q: What usually drives the price of a memecoin?
questions.explain: Memecoins are mostly speculation. When the hype is over, prices often crash.

questions.q: How many bitcoins can ever exist?
questions.explain: Bitcoin's supply is capped at 21 million coins.

posts.title: GEWINN Fair 2026: Careers, Austria's Economy and Money Mistakes
posts.excerpt: Notes from three talks at the GEWINN fair in Vienna: what to do after school, how Austria's economy is doing in global competition, and Gerald Hörhan on six common money mistakes.

content: On **Friday, 23 October 2026**, we visited the **GEWINN fair** in Vienna. We listened to three talks and took notes. Here is a summary of what we learned.
The first talk was about choosing a path after school. Questions we discussed:
- What do I want to study or work as?
- A degree from a university of applied sciences (FH) and a university degree are **equivalent**.
- Is Erasmus or going abroad worth it?
- How an FH studies programme can prepare you for a successful life.

blocks.label: Tips from the talk
content: - Get information everywhere you can.
- Being satisfied with what you do matters most.
- Follow your interests.
- Don't be afraid and be brave: there are many options.
- Always ask questions.
_Austria's economy in national and international competition, with Stefan Bruckbauer._
### What drives the economy right now
- **Energy prices, war and AI** are moving prices. Everyone wants AI, which needs a lot of investment and creates economic growth.
- China's exports of goods are **70% higher** than five years ago, while Europe's are **10% lower**.
- Gas is about **1.5 times** as expensive as before, oil about **twice** as expensive.
- Everything negative also hits Austria, but Germany is hit even harder.
### How is Austria doing?

According to the media, very badly, and real GDP growth seems to confirm it: Austria is doing worse than the European average. The main reason is the **construction sector**, where the boom has ended. Retail is also weak, while the public sector and industry are doing better.
In the USA, growth is driven almost only by AI, but around 80% of people do not benefit from it.

If you look at **consumer sentiment**, Austrians are actually better off than people in China or the USA. Still, people everywhere are as pessimistic as they have not been in 50 years, especially since Covid-19 (in the USA mainly because of tariffs and interest rates).
### Why interest rates have risen
1. **Inflation** caused by energy prices.
2. A lot of **new debt**, especially because of AI investment.
On the positive side, AI will make each worker more **productive**.
### Energy

Everyone is worried about not having enough energy, because gas storage levels are the lowest in 25 years. The speaker's point: we should switch to green energy not only because of climate change, but because fossil energy keeps getting more expensive.
### The global picture
- Half of the world's stock market is moved by only **25 companies**. AI will work, but can companies really earn that much money with it? If someone offers it cheaper, the stock market could shake.
- **Every third good** in the world is produced in China, and **every third service** comes from the USA.
- Europe already pays more to the USA for IT and software than it earns from exporting goods there. The USA also dominates in space.

- The USA is so dominant because it has so much capital: US companies are worth about **10 times** as much on the stock market as European ones. But about **10%** of the US stock market is owned by Europeans.
- The US boom mostly benefits companies and their owners: **10% of the population** receive **80%** of the dividends.
Austria has to save more because of its debt, but it is still doing better than the European average.

blocks.label: Conclusion
content: Overall, things don't look too bad: there will be more growth and less inflation. But there are big challenges. Companies have to become more dynamic, Europe has to respond to cheap imports from China, and in the EU society is more equal than in the USA or China.

blocks.text: 3. Gerald Hörhan: Succeeding in wild times

content: _Gerald Hörhan (Investment Punk Academy) on how to be successful in uncertain times._

His starting point: you have to know **what you want, what you don't want, and where you want to go**. He told us that at 12 or 13 he looked at how most people live and decided he wanted money and a good life. His motto: _"Never bow to anybody."_
### His advice
- Work hard and choose an industry where you can earn money.
- AI will replace jobs in many areas, so think about where future-proof jobs are.
- Consider becoming an **entrepreneur**: lower taxes and more sources of income.
- Understand **tax law**, so the state doesn't take everything.

- Don't waste your money: in his view, buying your own home is the biggest financial mistake of the middle class. Instead, buy a small one-room flat regularly and rent it out. Don't buy a new car either, because it loses more than half of its value in three years.
- **Invest in a structured way.**
### Six financial mistakes
1. Buying a home on credit far out in the countryside
2. Consumer debt
3. Believing your employee job is safe
4. Not understanding taxes
5. Expensive relationships and divorce
6. Not understanding AI
### AI and the future

He believes AI will soon make many decisions for us, from dates to cars and travel. We should become the people who **build the algorithms and AI models** and keep our own logical thinking. In his view, this will be the industry where the most money is made, also in Europe. Everyone should try coding with AI, and use a second AI tool to check the results.
He also said that school did not help him much, except for logical thinking, discipline, and economics and accounting.

blocks.label: His four rules
content: - Stay healthy
- Be honest
- Use your full potential
- Get rich

posts.title: Visit to WU Vienna: FMA Breakfast & Classmate Interview
posts.excerpt: We attended the 3rd Financial Education Breakfast of WU Vienna and the Austrian Financial Market Authority (FMA), all about financial fraud. Afterwards I interviewed a classmate about what we learned.

content: On **6 November 2026** our Economics class visited **WU Vienna** (Vienna University of Economics and Business) for the **3rd Financial Education Breakfast** (Finanzbildungsfrühstück). It was organised by the **WU Competence Center for Financial Literacy** and the **Austrian Financial Market Authority (FMA)** in Festsaal 1 of the LC building on the WU campus.
### Topic: financial fraud

How can you tell serious financial offers from dubious ones? This question no longer affects only adults. **Young people are more and more often targeted by fraudsters.** That is why this breakfast focused on **financial fraud**: experts showed current developments and how students can learn to recognise scams.
The event is based on a cooperation between WU and the FMA: the FMA's series **"Reden wir über Geld"** ("Let's talk about money") is turned into teaching material for schools by WU.

blocks.label: Programme
content: - **09:00** Arrival and first coffee
- **09:10** Welcome: a member of the WU rectorate, Bettina Fuhrmann (WU Vienna) and Fiona Springer (FMA)
- **09:20** _Your money. Your decision. Your future._ Financial education as the key to self-determination and independence. Martina Künsberg Sarre (Member of the National Council)
- **09:30** _Financial education is education for life._ Let's talk about money and our future. Mariana Kühnel (FMA)
- **09:40** _Financial fraud: you never stop learning._ Fiona Springer and Patricia Floh-Weninger (FMA)
- **10:00** _On the trail of fraud:_ the work of the Federal Criminal Police Office (Bundeskriminalamt)
- **10:20** _On the trail of fraud:_ what students can (and should) recognise. Alexander Pittesser (BHAK10, WU Vienna)
- **11:00** Discussion with rolls and refreshments

posts.title: How Does the Economy Work?
posts.excerpt: Our whiteboard explainer video: from wants and resources to the circular flow of income, supply and demand, GDP, the business cycle, and the role of jobs, banks, politics and trade.

content: For this team assignment we made a short video that explains **how the economy works**. We drew each idea step by step on the whiteboard.

blocks.label: Key points
content: 1. **Wants & resources:** people have unlimited wants, but resources are limited (scarcity).
2. **Circular flow of income:** households and firms exchange money, goods, services and work.
3. **Supply & demand:** price and quantity meet at the market equilibrium.
4. **Systems & GDP:** GDP = C + I + G + (X − M), with consumer spending, investment, government spending, exports and imports.
5. **Business cycle & inflation:** expansion, peak and recession, and how prices rise.
6. **Jobs, banks, politics & trade:** the actors that keep the economy running.

questions.q: What does the G in GDP = C + I + G + (X − M) stand for?
questions.explain: C is consumer spending, I investment, G government spending, X exports and M imports.

questions.q: What happens at the market equilibrium?
questions.explain: At equilibrium the quantity supplied equals the quantity demanded.

questions.q: Which phase comes after the peak of a business cycle?
questions.explain: After the peak, the economy slows down and can fall into a recession.

posts.title: OeNB Debate: Competitiveness, Prosperity and Quality of Life
posts.excerpt: Panel discussion at the Austrian National Bank (OeNB) on competitiveness, prosperity and quality of life. I prepared four questions and got to ask the panel mine about the digital euro.

content: On **22 October 2026** we attended a panel discussion at the **Oesterreichische Nationalbank (OeNB)** in the Kassasaal, from 17:30 to 20:30. The title was:
> Motoren der Wettbewerbsfähigkeit, des Wohlstands und der Lebensqualität? _(Engines of competitiveness, prosperity and quality of life?)_

blocks.label: The panel
content: - **Hans Bürger:** domestic politics expert at ORF, author (moderator)
- **Leonore Gewessler:** Member of Parliament, federal spokesperson of the Greens, former Minister for Climate Protection and Infrastructure
- **Barbara Kolm:** Member of Parliament, FPÖ economic spokesperson, long-time Vice President of the OeNB
- **Ralf Kronberger:** chief economist of the Austrian Economic Chamber (WKO), member of the Fiscal Advisory Council
- **Christoph Matznetter:** Member of Parliament, SPÖ economic spokesperson, former State Secretary in the Ministry of Finance
- **Matthias Schnetzer:** chief economist of the Chamber of Labour (AK)
- **Madlen Stottmeyer:** chief reporter at Die Presse
- How could a **digital euro** affect the prosperity of the population?
- How are **competitiveness, prosperity and quality of life** connected, and do they sometimes contradict each other?
- Does more economic prosperity automatically mean a better quality of life, or do other factors matter just as much or even more?

blocks.label: The question I asked live
content: ### I got to ask this question to the panel
> When I pay with cash, I stay anonymous. Is there a concrete legal guarantee that the digital euro will not become a tool that makes every payment fully traceable, including by future governments?
I also prepared three more questions:
2. Austria's GDP per capita is high, but many people still feel poorer. Does GDP still measure what people actually experience as prosperity, such as housing costs, time and health?

3. If you had one sentence for young people in training or an apprenticeship today: will they be better off in Austria in 20 years than their parents? And what has to happen in the next few years for that?
4. AI and digitalisation bring productivity, but also more surveillance and fewer jobs in some areas. How do you make sure the gains in prosperity reach people and not only big companies?
### The crisis in France
At the start, the panel talked about the crisis in France, which was a very hot topic in October.
### China: work vs. quality of life

Is China only so successful because people there focus almost entirely on work, while in Austria we also value enjoying life? This connects directly to the main question: a more competitive economy does not automatically mean a higher quality of life.
### The digital euro
Will the digital euro run into problems in the future? And could it help Europe become **less dependent on American payment providers** such as Visa, Mastercard or PayPal?
### Hidden champions

Austria has many **hidden champions**: companies that most people have never heard of, but that produce a lot and are often world market leaders in a small niche. The panel discussed how important these firms are for Austria's economy and jobs.

makingOf.intro: This website was built with Claude, an AI assistant by Anthropic. I never edited HTML or CSS myself. I wrote prompts, sent my texts, videos and notes, and Claude built and updated the site. All posts live in one simple data file, posts.json, and every change goes online through GitHub Pages.

prompts.label: The first prompt
prompts.text:
Create a modern, clean, and responsive Economics blog and portfolio website in English for my school assignments (similar in structure to modern Wix economics blogs, but with a much cleaner, faster, and more contemporary design).

1. Structure & Navigation:
- Header: Website title 'Economics Portfolio' (or 'Economics with [MY FIRST NAME]') and a clean navigation bar.
- Categories / Topics: Include a filterable overview and menu structure for core economics topics: All Posts, Introduction, Markets, Money, Business Cycles, Sustainability, Europe, International, and Excursions & Events.
- Media Support: The blog must easily support multiple assignment formats: text articles, embedded videos (MP4 files or YouTube links), audio/podcasts (MP3 players), and embedded presentations (PDFs or slides).

2. First Assignment (Ready to go):
Create the very first blog post as a featured article right at the top of the page:
- Title: 'Visit to WU Vienna: FMA Breakfast & Classmate Interview'
- Category: Excursions & Events (and Money)
- Date: November 2026
- Content: Include a clean placeholder section for our filmed video interview with a classmate about our visit to the WU (Vienna University of Economics and Business) and the FMA (Financial Market Authority) Breakfast, plus a structured text section below the video titled 'FMA Focus Area' where I can easily paste my notes from the class handout.

3. Super Easy Workflow for Future Assignments:
I do not want to edit HTML or CSS myself. Store all posts in a single, super simple data file (like posts.json or separate Markdown files in a posts/ folder). When I give you new texts, videos, podcasts, or presentations in the future and say 'Add this as a new assignment', you will update the site automatically.

4. Setup:
Build the site using simple, reliable web technologies (HTML, CSS, vanilla JavaScript) so it can be hosted for free anywhere (like GitHub Pages or Netlify). Start a local preview server so I can view it right away, and briefly explain how I can drop in my interview video file.

5. If you have any questions, please ask before you start.
